clue.text: Conceal grease, which is found in margarine

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

parts.note: to palm something is to hide it in the hand
grease and oil are both lubricants

explanation.surface: A cook hides fat in a recipe, the kind that ends up in margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: This vegetable fat from oil palm fruit is a major ingredient of many margarine spreads.

clue.text: Chart used in aeroplanes

indicators.note: used in says the letters sit inside the following word

parts.note: found within the word, after AERO

explanation.surface: A map that pilots use in their aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing or diagram, such as a floor layout or map, is both a chart and this word.

clue.text: False or true, heartless Bavarians sport them

indicators.note: false means not genuine, so the letters are not in their true order

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Whether loyal or cruel, Bavarian men wear a certain garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' looks like a deletion signal, but every letter of it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Lederhosen, short breeches made of hide, are traditional dress in Bavaria in southern Germany.

clue.text: Agreed about books I see can be bought without cash

definitions.note: a phrase describing how goods are bought; the answer is an adverbial phrase

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for agreed wraps around what follows

parts.note: OK signals agreement
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
taken as written
the letter C is pronounced like see

explanation.surface: Agreement concerning books one notices that may be had on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying on tick is a British idiom for buying on credit, paying later rather than in cash now.

clue.text: Permit pilot to lose his temper

parts.note: to let is to permit
to pilot an aircraft is to fly it

explanation.surface: Allowing an airman to get angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To let fly is to unleash a verbal attack, an idiom for an angry outburst.

clue.text: Stuff good pig meat with alcohol first

indicators.note: first tells us the alcohol is placed at the front, ahead of the other pieces

parts.note: gin is a spirit
G is the standard abbreviation for good
ham is cured meat from a pig's leg

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction: stuff pork with booze before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like a cooking verb but is the definition, a noun meaning cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuff is an old word for woven fabric, and this checked cotton cloth is one such material.

clue.text: Bright as Garry?

parts.note: surface reading: as clever or cheerful as someone named Garry
setter's reading: like the glam-rock singer Gary of sparkling stage costumes

explanation.walkthrough: Gary Glitter was a 1970s British glam-rock star; the question mark flags the play on his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sparkling with shiny flecks is bright, and the adjective comes from that singer's stage surname.

clue.text: Becoming aware there's no time before decorating

indicators.note: before places the time piece ahead of the decorating piece

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time
icing a cake is decorating it

explanation.surface: Realising there's no time left before you paint the house.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice is to become conscious of something, so the present participles match.

clue.text: This complex illness is certainly not funny

parts.words: This complex illness is certainly not funny
parts.note: surface reading: a serious medical condition is no laughing matter
setter's reading: the first word usually means very funny, so it is a joke to call the illness not funny

explanation.surface: A grave remark that a complicated disease is no joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' hints at a psychological complex: the fever is nervous in origin, though its name sounds like a laugh riot.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old medical term for a feverish state arising from nervous or emotional disturbance rather than infection.

clue.text: Unlucky Mexican emperor was mistakenly lax in Miami

indicators.note: done mistakenly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A doomed ruler of Mexico made the error of relaxing in Florida.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian archduke installed as Emperor of Mexico in 1864 was overthrown and executed by firing squad in 1867.

clue.text: A very extensive maritime order

parts.note: taken as written
something vast is very extensive

explanation.surface: A huge naval command is being described.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors shout this command to tell someone to stop or hold fast, an instruction used at sea.

clue.text: (and 10 again) Perfect figures

parts.note: surface reading: flawless numbers, or numbers that are perfect in the mathematical sense
setter's reading: the bust, waist and hip measurements of the ideal female body, with this one repeated at the end

explanation.walkthrough: The ideal vital statistics are 36-24-36 inches; this entry and 12's first word make the first two, and '(and 10 again)' supplies the third. The printed enumeration covers more than this nine-letter light.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure is a body shape, and the classic perfect female figure measures thirty-six inches at bust and hips.

clue.text: Sweet brown ointment

parts.note: chocolate is a shade of brown
a cream is a soothing ointment

explanation.surface: A pleasant-sounding brown balm for the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a confection with a soft fondant centre coated in chocolate, the kind found in boxes of sweets.

clue.text: Continuous numbers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: around the clock, every hour of every day
second meaning: literally two numbers, hours in a day and days in a week

explanation.walkthrough: It is written 24/7, from twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for non-stop or all the time, and it is made of two numerals.

clue.text: Twist a rope

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bend out of shape
second meaning: a nautical line used to haul a ship along

explanation.surface: An instruction for making rope by twisting strands.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber warps when it bends out of true, and sailors also use the word for a hawser for moving a vessel.

clue.text: Post often delivered before or about dinner

parts.note: surface reading: the mail tends to arrive ahead of the evening meal
setter's reading: the prefix post- is often put in front of this word, as in an after-dinner speech

explanation.surface: The postman usually comes before dinner time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' is not mail but the Latin prefix meaning after, which commonly precedes this adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Latin prandium, a meal, so it describes things relating to a dinner or lunch.

clue.text: Making holes in a blacksmith's fastener

indicators.note: making means constructing, so the letters are built into something new

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A smith punches holes in metal to fix a horseshoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making holes' reads as the smith's punching action, but 'Making' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrier hammers such small spikes through a horseshoe into the hoof to hold it in place.

clue.text: Unknown clergyman returned with complicated tale, long overdue

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so this pair is read backwards

parts.note: in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns
Rev is short for Reverend

indicators.note: complicated means tangled, so the following letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A mysterious vicar comes back with a convoluted story that is well past due.
explanation.definitionFit: Something long overdue has been delayed far beyond its expected time.

clue.text: It's Athens or bust to find a source of oil and gas

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so those letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A prospector heads to Greece, all or nothing, hunting for fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Athens or bust' reads like a travelling motto; 'bust' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Since the 1970s this stretch of water off Britain and Norway has been a major offshore petroleum field.

clue.text: A simple, but not basic, language of Indonesia

parts.words: A simple, but not basic, language of Indonesia
parts.note: surface reading: an easy tongue spoken in Indonesia
setter's reading: a computer programming language that is not BASIC, sharing its name with an Indonesian island

explanation.surface: Describing an easy but sophisticated Indonesian tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: BASIC is an old beginners' programming language; the answer is another programming language, also the name of Indonesia's most populous island.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a widely used programming language and also the main island of Indonesia, home to Jakarta.

clue.text: Begin working in time and (reportedly) earn, too

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so these words are taken by their sound

parts.note: a vessel's name said the same way as this word
said identically

explanation.surface: Starting work promptly and also earning money.
explanation.walkthrough: Earn and urn sound alike in a non-rhotic British accent.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn to is an idiom for setting to work energetically.

clue.text: Stella gets ready

indicators.note: gets is read as becomes, so the name is turned into something else

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: A woman called Stella prepares herself.
explanation.definitionFit: Being completely prepared to start is what this informal phrase means.

clue.text: I am 100% sure, though the risk's not really mine

parts.note: surface reading: a plain statement of total certainty

parts.words: though the risk's not really mine
parts.note: setter's reading: the phrase literally has the listener wager their own existence, not the speaker

explanation.surface: Someone declares absolute certainty while noting someone else bears the risk.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom is an emphatic way of saying certainly, although literally it stakes the other person's existence.

clue.text: Just, but onerously disheartened

indicators.note: disheartened says the heart, the middle part of the word, is taken out

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fair outcome, though dispiriting and burdensome.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle five letters are cut out, leaving two at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: Just as an adverb means merely or no more than, the same sense as this word.

clue.text: I gave Nora trouble once more

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to bothering Nora yet another time.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean repeating something a second time, so they are synonyms for doing it afresh.

clue.text: See 12
Employers, ignoring one member, brewed a cuppa

indicators.note: brewing stirs things together, so what is left is mixed into a new order
to ignore something is to leave it out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Bosses, minus one of their number, made a pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosy Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, which is what a cuppa is in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang this phrase rhymes with tea, so it names a cup of that hot drink.

clue.text: Essential equipment for office in public board

parts.note: something out is in the open, publicly known
a tray is a flat board for carrying things

explanation.surface: Office kit required by a public body's board.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk receptacle holding finished papers waiting to be sent on is standard kit in any workplace.
